quests.hint: Listen for which season she visited France.
quests.explanation: 'Summer' and 'spring' are different seasons. 'Last summer' means the most recent summer; 'last spring' means the most recent spring. Season + time expressions are very common in English storytelling.
quests.textToSpeak: She visited France for the first time last summer.
quests.correctAnswer: She visited France for the first time last spring.

quests.hint: Pay attention to how old he was when he learned to drive.
quests.explanation: 'Eighteen' and 'seventeen' sound similar in fast speech. In the UK, the legal driving age is seventeen - cultural knowledge like this helps you understand context and remember vocabulary.
quests.textToSpeak: He learned to drive when he was eighteen.
quests.correctAnswer: He learned to drive when he was seventeen.

quests.hint: Notice where they first met each other.
quests.explanation: A 'wedding' is a marriage ceremony; a 'party' is a social gathering. Both are social events where people meet. 'They met at a...' uses the past simple for a specific completed event.
quests.textToSpeak: They met each other at a friend's wedding.
quests.correctAnswer: They met each other at a friend's party.

quests.hint: Listen for the colour of the jacket she recommends.
quests.explanation: 'Blue' and 'red' are both common jacket colours. When giving opinions about clothes, 'I think the [colour] [item] looks better' is a natural, polite way to express a preference.
quests.textToSpeak: I think the blue jacket looks better on you.
quests.correctAnswer: I think the red jacket looks better on you.

quests.hint: Focus on what is too much about the city - noise or cost.
quests.explanation: 'Too noisy' and 'too expensive' are two very different complaints about a city. 'In my opinion, this city is too...' is a great phrase for expressing opinions - 'in my opinion' signals a personal view, not a fact.
quests.textToSpeak: In my opinion, this city is too noisy.
quests.correctAnswer: In my opinion, this city is too expensive.

quests.hint: Notice what she believes is important for health - exercise or sleep.
quests.explanation: Both 'exercise' and 'sleep' are important for health, but they're different. 'She believes that...' uses a that-clause - a key grammar structure for reporting opinions. 'Believe' is slightly more formal than 'think'.
quests.textToSpeak: She believes that exercise is important for health.
quests.correctAnswer: She believes that sleep is important for health.

quests.hint: Listen for whether the summer was cold or warm.
quests.explanation: 'Cold' and 'warm' describe temperature, but 'unusually cold' implies it was colder than expected. The adverb 'unusually' adds a layer of comparison. Weather descriptions using 'unusually' are very common in English.
quests.textToSpeak: The summer was unusually cold this year.
quests.correctAnswer: The summer was unusually warm this year.

quests.hint: Notice what type of weather caused problems on the roads.
quests.explanation: 'Strong winds' and 'heavy snow' both cause road problems, but in different ways. In English, weather expressions have fixed collocations: 'heavy snow/rain', 'strong/high winds'. Learning these pairs improves your naturalness.
quests.textToSpeak: Strong winds caused problems on the roads.
quests.correctAnswer: Heavy snow caused problems on the roads.

quests.hint: Pay attention to which season she prefers.
quests.explanation: 'Autumn' and 'spring' are both transitional seasons. In British English, the season is 'autumn' (not 'fall'). 'She prefers + noun + because of...' is a useful structure for explaining preferences with reasons.
quests.textToSpeak: She prefers autumn because of the changing leaves.
quests.correctAnswer: She prefers spring because of the changing leaves.

quests.hint: Listen for where he buys his clothes - same shop or online.
quests.explanation: 'From the same shop' and 'online' are two very different buying habits. 'Online shopping' is now one of the most common topics in English conversation. 'He always buys online' is a natural modern sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: He always buys his clothes from the same shop.
quests.correctAnswer: He always buys his clothes online these days.

quests.hint: Notice whether the new collection arrived last week or this week.
quests.explanation: 'Last week' refers to the week before the current one; 'this week' refers to the current week. This simple time distinction is critical for understanding when events happen relative to the present.
quests.textToSpeak: The new collection arrived in stores last week.
quests.correctAnswer: The new collection arrived in stores this week.

quests.hint: Focus on what she found - shoes or a bag.
quests.explanation: 'Shoes' and 'bag' are both fashion accessories. Notice that 'shoes' is plural (you always buy a pair) while 'bag' is singular. This grammatical difference is important and natural in English.
quests.textToSpeak: She found the perfect shoes at a great price.
quests.correctAnswer: She found the perfect bag at a great price.

quests.hint: Listen for which day the dinner party is planned.
quests.explanation: 'Saturday' and 'Sunday' are both weekend days. 'We are planning a dinner party for...' uses the present continuous for future arrangements - one of the most common ways to talk about plans in English.
quests.textToSpeak: We are planning a dinner party for Saturday.
quests.correctAnswer: We are planning a dinner party for Sunday.

quests.hint: Notice whether she wants a new job or a promotion.
quests.explanation: A 'new job' means moving to a different company or role; a 'promotion' means moving up within your current company. Both are career ambitions. 'She is thinking of applying for a...' is a great phrase for discussing career plans.
quests.textToSpeak: She is thinking of applying for a new job.
quests.correctAnswer: She is thinking of applying for a promotion.

quests.hint: Focus on whether they are going to paint or decorate the kitchen.
quests.explanation: 'Paint' specifically means applying paint to walls; 'decorate' is a broader word covering painting, wallpaper, and furnishings. 'Going to + verb' is the standard structure for concrete future plans.
quests.textToSpeak: They are going to paint the kitchen next month.
quests.correctAnswer: They are going to decorate the kitchen next month.

quests.hint: Pay attention to what surrounds the village.
quests.explanation: 'Mountains' and 'forests' are both natural landscapes. 'Surrounded by' uses the passive voice - 'the village is surrounded by mountains' is a natural way to describe geography in English.
quests.textToSpeak: The village is surrounded by beautiful mountains.
quests.correctAnswer: The village is surrounded by beautiful forests.

quests.hint: Listen for whether the hotel pool is outdoor or indoor.
quests.explanation: 'Outdoor' means outside in the open air; 'indoor' means inside a building. Both are common adjectives for facilities. 'The hotel has an outdoor/indoor...' is a typical phrase when describing accommodation.
quests.textToSpeak: The hotel has an outdoor swimming pool.
quests.correctAnswer: The hotel has an indoor swimming pool.

quests.hint: Notice whether the restaurant is in or near the town centre.
quests.explanation: 'In the town centre' means right at the heart of the town; 'near the town centre' means close by but not exactly there. Prepositions of place like 'in' and 'near' change meaning significantly.
quests.textToSpeak: The restaurant is located in the town centre.
quests.correctAnswer: The restaurant is located near the town centre.

quests.hint: Listen for whether it was the best or worst holiday.
quests.explanation: 'Best' and 'worst' are the superlative forms of 'good' and 'bad'. 'It was the best/worst holiday I have ever had' uses the present perfect with a superlative - a very common English structure for extreme experiences.
quests.textToSpeak: It was the best holiday I have ever had.
quests.correctAnswer: It was the worst holiday I have ever had.

quests.hint: Focus on how many countries she has worked in.
quests.explanation: 'Five' and 'three' are very different numbers. 'She has worked in five/three countries' uses the present perfect to describe life experience - a key grammar point for talking about what you have done in your life.
quests.textToSpeak: She has worked in five different countries.
quests.correctAnswer: She has worked in three different countries.

quests.hint: Notice whether he tried surfing or sailing.
quests.explanation: 'Surfing' means riding ocean waves on a board; 'sailing' means travelling on water using wind and a boat. Both are water sports. 'He tried [sport] for the first time' is a natural phrase for new experiences.
quests.textToSpeak: He tried surfing for the first time in Portugal.
quests.correctAnswer: He tried sailing for the first time in Portugal.

quests.hint: Listen for whether the food she dislikes is spicy or salty.
quests.explanation: 'Spicy' means containing strong flavours from spices; 'salty' means containing too much salt. Both describe food flavour. 'She cannot stand eating...' uses 'cannot stand + verb-ing' - a strong expression of dislike.
quests.textToSpeak: She cannot stand eating spicy food at all.
quests.correctAnswer: She cannot stand eating salty food at all.

quests.hint: Notice whether he prefers home cooking or eating out.
quests.explanation: 'He prefers home-cooked meals to eating out' and 'he prefers eating out to home-cooked meals' are complete opposites. 'Prefer A to B' is the standard structure for comparing preferences in English.
quests.textToSpeak: He prefers home-cooked meals to eating out.
quests.correctAnswer: He prefers eating out to home-cooked meals.

quests.hint: Focus on where the restaurant gets its fresh ingredients.
quests.explanation: 'Local farms' and 'local markets' are both sources of fresh food. Describing where ingredients come from is very trendy in modern English. 'Uses fresh ingredients from...' is a common phrase in restaurant descriptions.
quests.textToSpeak: The restaurant uses fresh ingredients from local farms.
quests.correctAnswer: The restaurant uses fresh ingredients from local markets.

quests.hint: Listen for what people check first thing in the morning.
quests.explanation: Checking 'phones' and checking 'emails' are related habits but not the same. Many people check their phone for emails, social media, and messages. 'First thing in the morning' is a common time expression in English.
quests.textToSpeak: Most people check their phones first thing in the morning.
quests.correctAnswer: Most people check their emails first thing in the morning.

quests.hint: Notice whether online shopping or banking has made life easier.
quests.explanation: 'Online shopping' and 'online banking' are both digital services. 'Has made life much easier' uses the present perfect with a result - a very natural structure in English for discussing the impact of modern technology.
quests.textToSpeak: Online shopping has made life much easier.
quests.correctAnswer: Online banking has made life much easier.

quests.hint: Focus on what she spends too much time on.
quests.explanation: 'Social media' and 'her phone' overlap but are not identical - you can use a phone for many things beyond social media. 'Spend too much time on...' is a common phrase for discussing unhealthy habits.
quests.textToSpeak: She spends too much time on social media.
quests.correctAnswer: She spends too much time on her phone.

quests.hint: Listen for which subject he studied at university.
quests.explanation: 'Engineering' and 'economics' are both university subjects but in completely different fields. When talking about education, 'He studied + subject + at + university' is the standard English structure.
quests.textToSpeak: He studied engineering at a top university.
quests.correctAnswer: He studied economics at a top university.

quests.hint: Notice whether she was the best or youngest student.
quests.explanation: 'Best student' describes academic performance; 'youngest student' describes age. Both use superlative adjectives. Distinguishing between these two very different compliments requires careful listening.
quests.textToSpeak: She was the best student in her year group.
quests.correctAnswer: She was the youngest student in her year group.

quests.hint: Pay attention to what the school introduced - technology or new methods.
quests.explanation: 'Technology' refers to devices and digital tools; 'methods' refers to teaching approaches and strategies. Both describe classroom change. 'The school introduced new...' is a natural sentence pattern for describing institutional change.
quests.textToSpeak: The school introduced new technology in the classrooms.
quests.correctAnswer: The school introduced new methods in the classrooms.
